1.title: Batch Processing and Multi-Pass Review
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Batch Processing and Multi-Pass Review. This module covers task statements four point five and four point six: batch processing and multi-pass review. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. The Message Batches A P I (application programming interface): fifty percent cost savings, up to twenty-four hours, no latency guarantee, custom id. Which workflows are batch-friendly and which are blocking. S L A (service level agreement) arithmetic for submission windows, and how to resubmit failures. Self-review limits, independent instances, multi-pass reviews and confidence-based routing.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Wants a Smaller Bill
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Wants a Smaller Bill. Two Claude workflows run in real time: (one) a live chat translator that customers wait on, and (two) a weekly refresh of forty thousand product descriptions that is published on Monday. The finance team says: "Move both to the batch A P I and save fifty percent".

1.title: The Message Batches API
1.text: The Message Batches A P I. Saving. fifty percent of the standard price. Time. Results within up to twenty-four hours; many batches finish much sooner, but there is no guaranteed latency S L A. Matching (correlating) request and response pairs. custom id on each request (unique, one to sixty-four characters); results may come back in any order. Flow. Create the batch to poll its status until it has ended to read results by custom id. Tool calls. A batch request is one model call: the A P I cannot run a tool mid-request and send the result back (no multi-turn tool calling inside a single request).

1.title: The Message Batches API, continued
1.text: The Message Batches A P I, continued. The figure shows this: Match the A P I to the latency need: synchronous for blocking steps, batch for latency-tolerant work.

1.title: The Message Batches API, continued
1.text: The Message Batches A P I, continued. Live chat translation, pre-merge check (a person waits). Synchronous. Weekly product-description refresh, overnight technical-debt report. Batch. Weekly audit of documents. Batch. Nightly test generation. Batch. Anything that needs an agentic tool loop. Synchronous (loop in your code). Exam tip: "fifty percent cheaper" is not a reason to batch a blocking workflow. "Often finishes faster" is not an S L A.

1.title: The Message Batches API, continued
1.text: The Message Batches A P I, continued. Current documentation: most batches finish within an hour; results are available when all requests have finished or after twenty-four hours; a batch holds up to one hundred thousand requests or two hundred fifty-six megabytes; results stay downloadable for twenty-nine days. A batch may include requests that define tools, but each request still ends after one response, so there is no tool-execution round trip. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: Planning against an SLA
1.text: Planning against an S L A. Worst case wait equals time until the next submission plus the twenty-four-hour processing window. Example: data must be processed within a thirty-hour S L A. If you submit a batch every four hours, the worst case is four plus twenty-four equals twenty-eight hours, which meets the S L A with margin. Submitting once a day (twenty-four plus twenty-four equals forty-eight hours) does not.

1.title: Planning against an SLA, continued
1.text: Planning against an S L A, continued. The figure shows this: S L A arithmetic: submission interval plus the twenty-four-hour processing window must fit inside the S L A.

1.title: Handling failures and improving first-pass success
1.text: Handling failures and improving first-pass success. Some requests in a batch may fail (for example a document too long for the context window). Resubmit only the failed ones, found by custom id, with changes such as chunking the oversized document. Refine the prompt on a small sample first before submitting thousands of documents, to maximize first-pass success and reduce the cost of iterative resubmission. Exam tip: A blocking step (someone waits) is never a batch job; compute the interval as interval plus twenty-four hours at most S L A.

1.title: Why self-review is weak
1.text: Why self-review is weak. A model that just produced code retains its reasoning context, so in the same session it is less likely to question its own decisions. An independent review instance (no prior reasoning context) is more effective at catching subtle issues than telling the same session to "review carefully" or turning on extended thinking.

1.title: Multi-pass review
1.text: Multi-pass review. The figure shows this: Multi-pass review: per-file local passes, one cross-file integration pass, and a verification pass with confidence for routing.

1.title: Multi-pass review, continued
1.text: Multi-pass review, continued. Per-file local passes. Consistent depth on each file; avoids attention dilution. Cross-file integration pass. Cross-file data flow and interface issues. Verification pass. The model self-reports a confidence for each finding, enabling calibrated routing (low-confidence findings to human review). Exam tip: "Run it three times and keep only findings that appear twice" hides real bugs that a single run catches only sometimes. Prefer independent, differently scoped passes.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Batches A P I: fifty percent cheaper, up to twenty-four h, no latency S L A, custom id, poll for completion. Good for: Overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation. Bad for: Blocking work (pre-merge checks) and agentic tool loops. S L A math: Interval plus twenty-four h at most S L A (four h plus twenty-four h equals twenty-eight h at most thirty h). Failures: Resubmit only failed custom ids, chunk oversized docs. Before volume: Tune the prompt on a sample. Self-review: Weak: generator keeps its reasoning. Better: Independent instance, per-file passes plus integration pass, verification pass with confidence for routing.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The company proposes moving both the live chat translator and the weekly description refresh to the Message Batches A P I for the fifty percent saving. What is the best evaluation? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Batches may take up to twenty-four hours with no guaranteed latency, which suits the weekly refresh but not a customer who is waiting. The fallback design adds complexity that matching each workflow to the right A P I avoids.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. What identifies which batch result belongs to which request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Results can arrive in any order, so correlate with custom id.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Records must be processed within a thirty-hour S L A, and a batch takes up to twenty-four hours. What submission interval is safe? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Worst-case wait is the interval plus twenty-four hours; four plus twenty-four equals twenty-eight fits inside thirty. The other intervals break the S L A.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. In a batch of five hundred supplier contracts, eight fail because they exceed the context limit. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Resubmit failures only, with a modification that addresses the cause.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Before running twenty thousand documents through a batch, what should the team do to reduce rework? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Prompt refinement on a sample maximizes first-pass success and avoids expensive iterative resubmission.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Why can a batch request not drive a full agentic tool loop? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A tool round trip needs another request; a batch request ends after one response.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. The same session that wrote a function reviews it and reports "no issues", yet a colleague finds a subtle bug. What is the best architecture? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The generator's reasoning context makes self-review less critical; an independent instance catches more.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A team wants to send only uncertain review findings to a human. Which design supports that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Per-finding confidence enables routing of limited human attention (with calibration, covered in Module fourteen).

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two workloads suit the Message Batches A P I? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Batches suit latency-tolerant, non-blocking jobs. Anything a person or process waits on needs the synchronous A P I.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two practices strengthen a multi-pass review design? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Focused passes and an independent instance counter attention dilution and self-review bias. Consensus filtering hides real findings.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: C. Question five: D. Question six: D. Question seven: D. Question eight: C. Question nine: C and E. Question ten: A and B. In the next module, we continue the course.
